name: DaemonSet coverage + fix an unschedulable pod
objective: CKA › Workloads & Scheduling. Drill EVERY way to control where pods land, harder than the exam: node labels + nodeSelector, taints & tolerations (Equal + Exists), required and preferred nodeAffinity, pod anti-affinity spread, manual nodeName scheduling, DaemonSet coverage, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for an unschedulable pod. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: DaemonSet on every node
questions.teach:
A **DaemonSet** runs one copy of a pod on every matching node, adding/removing as nodes join/leave. Like a Deployment but with no `replicas`, and `spec.selector.matchLabels` must match the template labels.

**Gotcha:** control-plane nodes (and your tainted `$W1`) carry `NoSchedule` taints — to cover *every* node the template needs `tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]`, which tolerates all taints.
questions.prompt:
In `sched-learn` create DaemonSet `node-agent` (`busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`, label `app=node-agent`) with a toleration broad enough (`operator: Exists`) to run on **every** node including the control plane and the tainted `$W1`.

Target: `desiredNumberScheduled` == number of nodes and `numberReady` matches.
questions.hint: DaemonSet selector `app=node-agent`; template `tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]`. Verify with `kubectl -n sched-learn get ds node-agent` vs `kubectl get nodes`.
questions.solution:
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-agent
  namespace: sched-learn
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-agent
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: c
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

verification.description: DaemonSet node-agent runs one ready pod on every node

questions.eli5:
Think of a hotel where every floor needs its own ice machine — exactly one, on every floor, no exceptions. A **DaemonSet** is the manager that guarantees that: one copy of a pod on **every** node. Add a new floor (node), an ice machine appears automatically; remove the floor, it's gone. You never set a count — the count is simply "however many nodes there are."

That's the key difference from a Deployment: a Deployment has `replicas` (you pick a number); a DaemonSet has **no `replicas`** — it tracks the node count for you. This is how cluster-wide agents work: log collectors, monitoring agents, network plugins. Everything else about it looks like a Deployment (a `selector` plus a pod `template`, and the selector's labels **must** match the template's labels).

The catch is coverage. Some nodes hang "Keep Out" signs (**taints**) — the control-plane node always does, and in this lab a worker node is tainted too. A plain DaemonSet pod would be turned away from those nodes, so you'd get an ice machine on *most* floors but not all. To truly cover **every** node, the template carries `tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]`, a universal pass that ignores *all* taints.

**Watch out:**

- **Selector must match the template labels**, or the DaemonSet is rejected — just like a Deployment.
- **No `tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]` → tainted/control-plane nodes get skipped.** You'll see fewer pods than nodes.
- A DaemonSet has **no `replicas` field** — don't add one.
- Check coverage with `desiredNumberScheduled` vs `numberReady` (`kubectl get ds`) against `kubectl get nodes`.
- `operator: Exists` with **no key** tolerates everything; that's intentional here, but it's a very broad pass — don't use it casually on ordinary pods.
questions.deepDive:
## DaemonSet — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**A DaemonSet runs exactly one pod per matching node**, automatically adding a pod when a node joins and removing it when the node leaves. There is no `replicas` — the "replica count" is the number of eligible nodes.

### Minimal manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-agent
  namespace: sched-learn
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-agent          # MUST match template labels
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-agent        # matched by the selector
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists        # run on EVERY node, past all taints
      containers:
      - name: c
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sleep","3600"]
```

### DaemonSet vs Deployment
| | Deployment | DaemonSet |
|---|---|---|
| Count | `spec.replicas` (you choose) | one per eligible node (automatic) |
| Scheduled by | kube-scheduler | kube-scheduler (via `nodeAffinity` injected by the DS controller) |
| Scale command | `kubectl scale` | ❌ not scalable |
| Use case | stateless app, N copies | per-node agent (CNI, logs, metrics) |
| `selector` ↔ template labels | must match | must match |

### How it targets nodes
- **All nodes** by default.
- Restrict with **`spec.template.spec.nodeSelector`** or **nodeAffinity** in the template — the DS controller only creates pods for matching nodes.
- `desiredNumberScheduled` = number of nodes that match the DS's node constraints.

### Taints: why tolerations matter for coverage
To cover tainted nodes (control-plane, pressure conditions, your custom taint) the template needs tolerations. Real system DaemonSets add broad tolerations for exactly this reason.
```yaml
tolerations:
- operator: Exists            # tolerate ALL taints, all effects, all keys
```
Narrower alternatives:
```yaml
tolerations:
- key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
  operator: Exists
  effect: NoSchedule
```
> Kubernetes auto-adds some node-condition tolerations (e.g. `not-ready`, `unreachable`, disk/memory/PID pressure, `unschedulable`) to DaemonSet pods so per-node agents keep running. It does **not** auto-tolerate custom taints or the control-plane taint — you add those yourself.

### Status fields (coverage checks)
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `desiredNumberScheduled` | nodes that should run a pod |
| `currentNumberScheduled` | nodes that currently have one |
| `numberReady` | pods passing readiness |
| `numberAvailable` | ready + minReadySeconds met |
| `numberMisscheduled` | pods on nodes they shouldn't be on |

```bash
kubectl -n sched-learn get ds node-agent
kubectl -n sched-learn get ds node-agent -o jsonpath='{.status.desiredNumberScheduled}/{.status.numberReady}'; echo
kubectl get nodes --no-headers | wc -l       # compare to desiredNumberScheduled
kubectl -n sched-learn get pods -l app=node-agent -o wide
```

### Update strategy
| `spec.updateStrategy.type` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `RollingUpdate` (default) | delete+recreate pods gradually; tune `maxUnavailable` (and `maxSurge`) |
| `OnDelete` | new template applies only when you manually delete a pod |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No `replicas` field** — adding one is invalid. Don't `kubectl scale` a DaemonSet.
- **selector must equal template labels**, and `spec.selector` is **immutable** after creation.
- **Fewer pods than nodes?** Almost always a missing toleration (tainted/control-plane node) or a `nodeSelector`/affinity in the template that excludes nodes. Compare `desiredNumberScheduled` to the node count and check the uncovered node's taints.
- `operator: Exists` with **no key and no effect** tolerates *every* taint — exactly what "run everywhere" needs, but very broad for ordinary workloads.
- DaemonSet pods are scheduled by the normal scheduler (modern versions) using nodeAffinity the controller injects — they still respect resources and other taints you didn't tolerate.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n sched-learn get ds node-agent        # DESIRED == CURRENT == READY == #nodes
```
```yaml
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: node-agent } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: node-agent } }
    spec:
      tolerations: [ { operator: Exists } ]
      containers:
      - { name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sleep","3600"] }
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a pod that won't schedule
questions.teach:
A pod stuck `Pending` with **no node assigned** is a scheduling failure — run `kubectl describe pod

` and read **Events**: `0/N nodes are available` names the reason (a nodeSelector/affinity that matches nothing, or a taint with no toleration). **Gotcha:** fix the **Deployment template**, not the pod — the ReplicaSet recreates the pod, then confirm with `kubectl rollout status`.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `sched-diag` in `sched-learn` shows `0/1` — its pod is `Pending` and never schedules. Diagnose the scheduling fault and fix it so the Deployment reports an available replica. Don't delete and rebuild from scratch — find and fix what's wrong.

Target: Deployment `sched-diag` has at least 1 available replica.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n sched-learn describe pod -l app=sched-diag` → the events say no node matches its `nodeSelector` (disktype=nvme). Either remove that nodeSelector or point it at a label a node actually has, then watch `rollout status`.
questions.solution:
# describe shows: 0/3 nodes available — node(s) didn't match nodeSelector disktype=nvme.
# No node has disktype=nvme, so remove the impossible selector (an untainted node will take it).
kubectl -n sched-learn patch deployment sched-diag --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector"}]'
kubectl -n sched-learn rollout status deployment/sched-diag

verification.description: Deployment sched-diag has >=1 available replica (scheduling fault fixed)

questions.eli5:
Imagine a delivery driver who can't find any address that matches the order and just parks the truck, waiting. The package never arrives — not because anything crashed, but because the destination doesn't exist. A pod stuck `Pending` is that parked truck: the **scheduler** looked for a node that fits and found **none**, so the pod sits there, unassigned.

The good news: the scheduler leaves a note explaining exactly why. Run `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and read the **Events** at the bottom. You'll see a line like `0/3 nodes are available:` followed by the reason — "didn't match nodeSelector," "untolerated taint," "insufficient cpu," and so on. That sentence *is* the diagnosis.

In this lab the pod demands a node labeled `disktype=nvme`, but **no node has that label**, so it can never schedule. The fix is to make the requirement satisfiable: drop the impossible `nodeSelector` (or relabel/point it at a label a node actually has).

The crucial twist: this pod belongs to a **Deployment**. If you edit the live pod, the ReplicaSet just makes a fresh one with the same broken template. **You must fix the template** — patch the Deployment — so every future pod is correct. Then watch `kubectl rollout status` confirm it recovers.

**Watch out:**

- **`Pending` + no node = a scheduling problem.** Always start with `describe pod` → Events; don't guess.
- **Fix the Deployment template, not the pod.** Editing the pod is undone instantly by the ReplicaSet.
- A `Pending` pod can also mean **untolerated taint** or **not enough CPU/memory** — the Events tell you which.
- After patching, confirm with `rollout status` or `kubectl get deploy` showing an **available** replica — don't assume.
- **No scheduler Events at all?** Then `nodeName` was set manually (scheduler bypassed) — a different failure mode.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix an unschedulable pod — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**A pod `Pending` with no `nodeName` is a scheduling failure: the scheduler evaluated every node and none passed its filters.** The `describe pod` Events name the exact filter that failed; fix the *controller's template*, not the orphan pod.

### Step 1 — confirm it's a scheduling fault
```bash
kubectl -n sched-learn get pods -o wide        # STATUS Pending, NODE <none>
kubectl -n sched-learn describe pod <pod> | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
```
`Pending` + `NODE <none>` + a `FailedScheduling` event = scheduler couldn't place it.

### Step 2 — read the reason
The message format is `0/N nodes are available: <reasons>`. Common causes:

| Event fragment | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector` | `nodeSelector`/nodeAffinity matches no node | relabel a node, or relax/remove the selector |
| `had untolerated taint {k: v}` | node tainted, pod lacks toleration | add matching toleration (or untaint) |
| `Insufficient cpu` / `Insufficient memory` | requests exceed free capacity | lower requests, or add/free a node |
| `didn't match pod anti-affinity rules` | anti-affinity can't place it | add nodes, or soften to preferred |
| `node(s) were unschedulable` | node cordoned | `kubectl uncordon <node>` |
| `had volume node affinity conflict` | PV pinned to a different node | fix PV/zone or pod placement |

Here: **no node has `disktype=nvme`**, so the required `nodeSelector` is impossible.

### Step 3 — fix the TEMPLATE, not the pod
The pod is owned by a ReplicaSet owned by the Deployment. Editing the live pod is futile — the ReplicaSet recreates it from the (still broken) template. Patch the **Deployment**:
```bash
# Option A: remove the impossible nodeSelector
kubectl -n sched-learn patch deployment sched-diag --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector"}]'

# Option B: point it at a label a node actually has
kubectl -n sched-learn patch deployment sched-diag --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"disktype":"ssd"}}}}}'

# Option C (interactive): kubectl -n sched-learn edit deployment sched-diag
```
Patching the template triggers a rollout; the new ReplicaSet creates a schedulable pod.

### Step 4 — verify recovery
```bash
kubectl -n sched-learn rollout status deployment/sched-diag
kubectl -n sched-learn get deploy sched-diag      # READY 1/1, AVAILABLE 1
kubectl -n sched-learn get pods -o wide           # pod Running on a node
```

### Mental checklist for any Pending pod
1. `describe pod` → is there a **node assigned**? No → scheduling. Yes but not running → image/CrashLoop/volume, not scheduling.
2. Read the **FailedScheduling** reason verbatim — it's the answer.
3. Is the owner a **Deployment/DS/StatefulSet**? Fix the **template**, not the pod.
4. **Verify** with `rollout status` / `get deploy`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Editing the pod instead of the template** — the #1 trap. The ReplicaSet instantly undoes it. Patch/edit the Deployment.
- **`Pending` is not always scheduling.** A pod with a node assigned that won't start is an image pull / CrashLoopBackOff / volume-mount issue — different fix.
- **No Events at all** → `spec.nodeName` was set manually; the scheduler never saw it. Check the node name exists.
- **Don't delete-and-recreate** when asked to *fix* — you'd lose the point and the lesson; patch the existing object.
- `kubectl patch --type=json` with `remove` fails if the path doesn't exist — confirm the field is present first (`kubectl get deploy -o yaml`).
- After a fix, always confirm **AVAILABLE** (not just that a pod exists): readiness/resources can still block it.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n sched-learn describe pod -l app=sched-diag | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
kubectl -n sched-learn patch deployment sched-diag --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector"}]'
kubectl -n sched-learn rollout status deployment/sched-diag
```
